newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CRICKET-WARNE FACES CRUCIAL TEST ON INJURED FINGER.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-WARNE FACES CRUCIAL TEST ON INJURED FINGER.

text.p: Wrist spinner Shane Warne faces an examination on Friday that could determine Australia's fate against West Indies a fortnight before a ball is bowled in the opening test.

Warne, Australia's most potent bowler, makes his first-class debut as Victoria captain in the domestic Sheffield Shield this weekend in a match that assumes greater significance as a fitness test on his injured finger.
Unless Warne can prove his full recovery from surgery on his bowling hand, Australia may be reluctant to risk him in the Brisbane test, starting on November 22.
Warne, whose test haul stands at 207 wickets in 44 matches, has acknowledged the importance of the coming back-to-back Shield matches against New South Wales and then South Australia.
Even if he does play at the Gabba, doubts remain as to how much spin he will be able to impart on the ball for his stock leg-break delivery.
After months of discomfort, Warne opted for surgery in May to repair ligament damage in the ring finger of his right hand rather than endure repeated pain-killing injections.
He has not played in a first-class or international game since. During several pre-season matches for Victoria, he was reduced to bowling gentle medium pace to protect his finger.
Having been forced to withdraw from Australia's recent tours to Sri Lanka and India, Warne returned to bowl his alloted 10 overs in two recent domestic limited overs matches.
He took seven wickets at a total cost of 90 runs, but ominously, Warne had to put ice on the finger for 20 minutes afterwards.
"I'm slowly getting my confidence back," Warne said at the time. The finger is not too bad...I'll just keep doing what they keep telling me to."
But Warne knows better than most the huge difference between bowling a short spell in a one-day match and the physical rigours of test cricket.
Although few have said so openly, there is an underlying fear in Australian cricket that Warne's effectiveness as a test bowler -- if not his career itself -- could now be threatened.

"In the deepest recesses of his doubting self, he's wondering if he'll be able to bowl properly all season," Sydney Morning Herald cricket columnist and former Somerset captain Peter Roebuck wrote recently.

History is also not on Warne's side in the most exotic of the bowling arts. The immense strain on shoulder, wrist and spinning finger has curtailed many distinguished careers, including former Australian captain Richie Benaud who was finished at the age of 33.
"Shane Warne's wonky digit has broken the air of complacency around Australian cricket," Roebuck wrote.
"A single injury was all it took to expose Australia's frailties." he added in a reference to the loss in a one-day test in India last month.
On his return from India on Wednesday, Australia wicketkeeper Ian Healy said Warne's absence on tour had been telling.
"The Shane Warne factor was definitely missing. He doesn't only lift the confidence of our team and our bowlers but also does something to the opposition as well," Healy said.
When he takes the field at the Sydney Cricket Ground on Friday, Warne is due to face national captain Mark Taylor, the New South Wales opener.
Perhaps, just this once, the left-handed opener will not be overly disappointed if he loses his wicket -- so long as Warne is the man responsible.
